en.title: The Book of De · Chapter Twenty-one · Being Straight
en.原文:
亓正閔閔 亓民屯屯 亓正察察 亓邦夬夬 

禍 福之所倚 福 禍之所伏 孰知亓極 

亓无正也 正復為奇 善復為訞 

人之迷也 亓日固久矣 

是以方而不割 兼而不刺 直而不紲 光而不耀
en.字龕:
### 正 *zhèng* — the straight

**字 Graph** ｜ 篆 ![正之篆](/book-assets/hosuke-laozi-en/zhuan/%E6%AD%A3.svg)

**文 Gloss** ｜ The *Shuowen*: 「正，是也。從止，一以止。」 — "What is right. From 止, the foot, with 一, the line: the foot stopping at the line."

**像 Image** ｜ A foot arriving at a line — and stopping. The graph of rightness contains no ruler, no punishment, no code: only a walker who knows where to stop.

**義 Sense** ｜ This chapter's warning is built into the graph. 正 that stops at the line is straightness; 正 driven past the line — the sharp-eyed exactness of 察察 — has already turned 奇, strange. "The straight turns strange again": rightness overdriven is the very thing that breaks the state.

en.疏:
杳眇曰：

此章之要，在論政治寬猛之辨與禍福倚伏之理，而歸根於聖人方正之德。帛書、王弼二本之異，不可不察也。

夫「閔閔」與「悶悶」，皆寬簡之貌；「屯屯」與「淳淳」，皆厚實之貌。水之性柔，故能滋潤萬物而不爭；政治亦然，寬則民淳，猛則民缺。所謂「其政察察」者，峻法繁令、苛察之政也；无為而治者，法水之善利萬物而有靜，因民之自然而治之，此水善利萬物而有靜之旨也。

至若「兼而不刺」，帛書之文也；王弼本作「廉而不劌」。兼者，兼容並蓄之謂；廉者，廉隅方正之謂。兼者近道家之和，廉者近儒家之節。「兼而不刺」者，言聖人之量，廣而不侵也；「方而不割」者，方正而不傷物也；「光而不耀」者，聖德內含，不以明耀炫人也；「直而不紲」者，王弼本作「肆」，直道而行而不多暴於物也。

「亓无正也，正復為奇，善復為訞」——此即不爭故无尤之義也。夫人之有尤，由於爭；欲无尤者，必先去爭之心。此非相對主義，乃時變之觀——正善非恆質，乃隨時而變之位。禍福亦然，無絕對之禍，無絕對之福，所謂「禍，福之所倚；福，禍之所伏」，互為條件，如環無端。此乃物理如實之觀，非宿命之悲觀也。

「人之迷也，亓日固久矣」——人之迷執於禍福正邪久矣，老子不責之，但歎之。久迷難醒，故聖人不強醒人，乃以方不割、兼不刺、直不紲、光不耀自處。此四者皆有其體而斂其用——方者有邊而不以邊傷人，兼者能容而不以容制人，直者正而不以正暴人，光者明而不以明炫人。

考之德經之義，拘校上古中古下古大德之善言，以類相從而成。帛書無「聖人」二字，直云「是以方而不割」，其義彌深。蓋此方正之德，非聖人獨有，乃道之固然也。為而不爭，乃全德之終。不爭之心達於上下，則光而不耀之治成矣。
en.疏英:
Yaomiao says:

The crux of this chapter: the weighing of lenient against harsh in governing, and the truth of calamity and fortune leaning on each other — closing at the sage's De of squareness. Here silk text and Wang Bi differ in ways that must be watched.

閔閔 and Wang Bi's 悶悶 are both the look of mild simplicity; 屯屯 and 淳淳 are both the look of thick honesty. Water's nature is soft, so it moistens the ten thousand things without contending; governing is the same: lenient, and the people grow honest; harsh, and the people grow chipped. The 察察 government is the government of steep law and dense decree, of prying exactness. Governing by non-doing patterns itself on water, which benefits the ten thousand things and keeps still, ruling by the people's own self-so — the point of "water benefits the ten thousand things and keeps still."

As for 兼而不刺, that is the silk text; Wang Bi reads 廉而不劌, "edged but not gashing." 兼 is embracing — holding much together; 廉 is the honed corner — angular integrity. 兼 leans toward the Daoist's harmony, 廉 toward the Confucian's rectitude. Embracing-but-not-piercing names the sage's capacity — wide without invading. Square-but-not-cutting — upright without wounding. Shining-but-not-dazzling — the sage's De held within, never flashed to blind. Straight-but-not-binding (紲; Wang Bi reads 肆) — walking the straight way without forcing it on things.

"It has no fixed straightness: the straight turns strange again, the good turns uncanny again" — the sense of "not contending, hence without fault." Men's faults come of contending; to be faultless, first drop the contending heart. This is not relativism; it is the watching of times and turns: straight and good are not fixed essences but positions that move with the hour. So with calamity and fortune: no calamity is absolute, no fortune absolute; each leans on the other, each crouches inside the other, a ring without an end. This is the plain grain of things, not fatalist gloom.

"Men have been lost in this a long day indeed": lost in gripping calamity-and-fortune, straight-and-strange, and long lost. Laozi does not scold; he sighs. The long-lost are hard to wake, so the sage does not force men awake: he sets himself square without cutting, embracing without piercing, straight without binding, shining without dazzling. All four keep their substance and sheathe their use. **The square has edges and wounds no one with them; the embracing can hold and coerces no one with it; the straight is upright and bullies no one with it; the shining is bright and blinds no one with it.**

Examined against the making of the Book of De — collating the good words of highest De from high antiquity through middle and late, sorted kind by kind — the silk text lacks the two graphs 聖人 here, saying directly, "therefore: square, but cutting no one." The sense runs deeper for it: this De of squareness is not the sage's private property but the Dao's own grain. Doing without contending is the completion of De entire. When the uncontending heart reaches through high and low, the government of shining-without-dazzling stands complete.
en.英譯:
Its rule: muffled and mild (閔閔); its people: thick and true (屯屯). Its rule: sharp and searching (察察); its state: split and splintered (夬夬).

Calamity — what fortune leans on; fortune — where calamity crouches. Who knows where it ends?

It has no fixed straightness (正): the straight turns strange again; the good turns uncanny (訞) again.

Long indeed have men been lost in this.

Therefore: square, but cutting no one; embracing (兼), but piercing no one; straight, but binding no one (紲); shining, but dazzling no one.
